property_summary: After calling setL1BlockValues with the constant depositor address, the reference contract retains the initial depositorAccount as address(0), while the buggy version sets it to the caller, causing a subsequent call from a different address to fail the require in the buggy version but succeed in the reference.

After calling setL1BlockValues, the depositorAccount state variable remains zero address (unchanged) in the reference but is overwritten to msg.sender in the buggy version, causing the second call to setL1BlockValues to succeed in the reference but revert in the buggy version.

After a first call to setL1BlockValues by the constant DEPOSITOR_ACCOUNT, the reference version rejects a second call from a different sender because depositorAccount remains zero, while the buggy version updates depositorAccount to msg.sender, allowing the second call from a different sender to succeed.

After calling setL1BlockValues with msg.sender != depositorAccount, in the reference version the call reverts (depositorAccount remains the zero address), while the buggy version does not revert (it sets depositorAccount = msg.sender) — so claiming that the depositorAccount is unchanged after the call fails on the buggy version.
After calling setL1BlockValues with any address, depositorAccount should not be overwritten to msg.sender; in the reference it stays as address(0), in the buggy version it changes to msg.sender.

After deployment, the reference version has depositorAccount = 0x0 (because it is never set), but the second version sets depositorAccount = msg.sender in the constructor, so calling setL1BlockValues with the same sender reverts on the reference version (since it checks against the constant DEPOSITOR_ACCOUNT, not depositorAccount) but succeeds on the second version.

In the reference version, setL1BlockValues() reverts because depositorAccount is uninitialized (address(0)), while in the buggy version depositorAccount is set to msg.sender in the constructor, so setL1BlockValues() succeeds when called by the same address.

The reference contract allows anyone to call setL1BlockValues because depositorAccount is uninitialized (address(0)), while the buggy version initializes depositorAccount to msg.sender in the constructor, causing the require to revert when a different account calls setL1BlockValues.

After constructing C, the reference contract sets depositorAccount to the zero address (default), so calling setL1BlockValues with any msg.sender (e.g., address(this)) reverts; the buggy version sets depositorAccount = msg.sender in the constructor, so the same call succeeds.

After deployment, the reference version has depositorAccount == address(0) (uninitialized), so the first call to setL1BlockValues from the depositor constant address reverts because msg.sender (0xdead...) does not match depositorAccount (0x0); the second version initializes depositorAccount = msg.sender in the constructor, making the call succeed.
